part_title: Q Business Controls and Q Apps in Context
review_basis: Narration prepared from the AIF module 07 lesson map and historical/current product caveats. Original numbered WebP integrity is gated in workflow; image-by-image visual content review not independently completed in this session.

scenes.title: Q Business admin controls
scenes.narration: Administrative chat controls influence how an assistant responds, but they are not the same thing as source permissions. In the historical Q Business workflow, global controls governed broad response behavior and available features. Topic controls could customize behavior for a particular kind of question or for specified people and groups. For example, a company might provide a special response pattern for questions about expenses while maintaining a general response policy for other topics. These settings help organize the assistant experience, but they do not grant access to an expense report that the employee cannot open. Also distinguish Amazon Q Business application chat controls from Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Both involve controlling AI interactions, but they are different product configuration mechanisms with different supported policies and scopes. For a real application, test prohibited topics, grounding, and who can access each document separately. A good administrator validates behavior with test identities that have different permissions. Remember: response policy does not replace identity management or document access control.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Apps
scenes.narration: Amazon Q Apps illustrated how a non developer could describe a useful small workflow in natural language and create a lightweight application. Imagine a team member asking for a simple app that summarizes an approved project document, collects a few fields, and presents an organized result. Natural language makes building a prototype approachable, but the generated app still depends on the information and services it is allowed to use. Administrators govern who can create or use these apps, and any configured action or document connection needs its own permissions. A generated form is not automatically safe to publish. Inspect its outputs, validate sensitive information handling, and test it as an ordinary user before sharing it. The context is important: this course lesson presents Q Apps within Amazon Q Business. Because Q Business no longer accepts new customers according to the course's product update, learners building a new workplace solution should assess Amazon Quick and current migration options. Check: does no code mean no security review? Certainly not; the same access and data protection requirements still apply.
